etymology: From Old French catel, from Latin capitale, property or capital — the same root that gives English chattel, since in an agrarian society a man's herds simply were his capital. The Hebrew miqneh makes the identical connection from the other direction: it is formed from qānâh, to acquire, so that cattle are literally acquisitions. B'hēmâh is the wider word for beasts, particularly domestic ones, as distinguished from the wild beast of the field.
biblical_def: Cattle appear on the sixth day, made before man and pronounced good in their own right: “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good” (Gen 1:25). The verdict is given before man exists to make use of them, which establishes that their goodness is not a function of their usefulness. Ownership of them is God's and not the herdsman's, and the psalm states it in a line that has become proverbial: “For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills” (Psa 50:10) — spoken to men who imagined they were supplying God by sacrifice. Because the cattle are God's, they are covered by His law, and the fourth commandment extends the sabbath rest to them explicitly: “thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates” (Exo 20:10). The beast gets the day off, and the law that protects him is the same law that governs the household. Most striking of all is the last sentence of Jonah, where God ends His argument with the sulking prophet by naming the animals: should not I spare Nineveh, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, “and also much cattle?” (Jon 4:11). The mercy of God, closing the book, takes in the herds.
webster_summary: Beasts or quadrupeds kept for tillage, food, or profit — oxen, sheep, and the like; in Scripture the domestic beasts made good on the sixth day, owned by God upon a thousand hills, given rest by the fourth commandment, and named in God's mercy over Nineveh.
webster_full: CATTLE, n. 1. Beasts or quadrupeds in general, serving for tillage, or other labor, or for food to man.
2. In its primary sense, the word includes camels, horses, asses, and all the varieties of domestic animals.
3. In the United States, it is applied chiefly to bovine animals, as oxen, bulls, cows and their young.
4. In the Hebrew, from a root signifying to acquire; possessions or substance, the herds being the wealth of a pastoral people.
5. In Scripture, the cattle upon a thousand hills. Psalm 50. Nor thy cattle. Exod. 20. And also much cattle. Jonah 4.
corruption_summary: Animals are either elevated to the moral standing of persons, so that human dominion is treated as tyranny, or reduced to pure commodity, so that the creature's good is nothing and cruelty costs nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption abolishes the creational distinction between man and beast. Where animals are granted rights identical to human rights, or where human beings are described as merely one species among others with no special standing, Scripture is directly contradicted: only man is made in the image of God, only man is given dominion, and only for man did the Son of God become incarnate. The Lord Jesus settles the comparison plainly — are ye not much better than they? and, how much then is a man better than a sheep? To flatten that distinction is not compassion but confusion, and in practice it has repeatedly coincided with a diminished regard for human life rather than an enlarged regard for animal life.

The opposite corruption is the commercial one, and among the orthodox it is by far the commoner. Because man has dominion, it is inferred that the beast has no claim at all — that stewardship means unlimited use. Scripture says otherwise and legislates against it: a righteous man regardeth the life of his beast; the ox is not to be muzzled while he treads out the corn; the beast rests on the sabbath; the fallen animal of even an enemy must be helped up. The principle to recover is that dominion is a trust exercised under an Owner who declares the cattle upon a thousand hills to be His, and who ends the book of Jonah by naming the herds among the reasons for sparing a city. Cruelty to an animal is not an offence against the animal's rights; it is an offence against its Maker's.
roots_summary: Hebrew b'hēmâh is a beast, especially a domestic one; miqneh is cattle as acquired property, from qānâh, to acquire; bāqār is the herd of oxen. Greek ktēnos is a beast of burden or property.
roots_lines: Hebrew b'hēmâh (H929) — beast, cattle; the domestic animals as distinct from chayyâh, the wild beast of the field.
Hebrew miqneh (H4735) — cattle as possession or substance; from qānâh, to acquire or purchase, whence a man's herds are his capital.
Hebrew bāqār (H1241) — the herd, oxen; distinguished from tsō'n, the flock of sheep and goats.
Greek ktēnos (G2934) — a beast of burden or domestic animal, from ktaomai, to acquire; the beast on which the wounded man was set (Luk 10:34).
Hebrew b'hēmōth — the intensive plural of b'hēmâh, used in Job 40:15 of the great beast God bids Job consider.
usage: Of their creation and goodness: God made... cattle after their kind... and God saw that it was good (Gen 1:25).
Of God's ownership: every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills (Psa 50:10).
Of sabbath rest extended to them: thou shalt not do any work... nor thy cattle (Exo 20:10).
scriptures: Genesis 1:25
And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good.
Psalm 50:10
For every beast of the forest is mine, and the cattle upon a thousand hills.
Exodus 20:10

But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:
Jonah 4:11
And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city, wherein are more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?

etymology: From Old English bulluc, a diminutive of bull — a young bull. The Hebrew par denotes a young bull in its prime, and the fuller expression par ben-bāqār, a bullock the son of the herd, marks it as the most valuable single animal a man could bring. That value is the point: the bullock is the offering prescribed where the guilt is heaviest.
biblical_def: The bullock is the costliest of the ordinary sacrifices, and the law assigns it precisely where sin does the most damage. When the anointed priest sins, the offering required is not a lamb or a pigeon but the best of the herd: “If the priest that is anointed do sin according to the sin of the people; then let him bring for his sin, which he hath sinned, a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering” (Lev 4:3). The greater the office, the greater the reparation — because a priest's sin corrupts the very channel through which the people approach God. Yet Scripture never lets the ritual stand alone, and the prophets attack the assumption that God is supplied by the offering: “To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks” (Isa 1:11). The psalmist states the ranking that governs the whole system: “This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs” (Psa 69:31) — thanksgiving from a right heart outweighing the largest animal in the yard. And yet the sacrifices are not thereby abolished but reordered, for the same psalter promises that when the heart is right the altar will be used properly again: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar (Psa 51:19). Hebrews gives the reason the whole arrangement was provisional: if the blood of bulls and of goats sanctified to the purifying of the flesh (Heb 9:13), how much more the blood of Christ.
webster_summary: A young bull; in the Levitical law the costliest of the ordinary sacrifices, required for the sin of the anointed priest and of the whole congregation, and the type whose insufficiency Hebrews sets against the blood of Christ.
webster_full: BULLOCK, n. 1. An ox, or castrated bull; in the Scriptures, a young bull.
2. In the Levitical law, the chief of the offerings, appointed for the sin of the priest and of the whole congregation. Levit. 4.
3. The most costly of the beasts of the herd; whence the offering of bullocks denotes the fullest measure of sacrifice.
4. In the Hebrew, par, a young bull in his strength; also a bullock the son of the herd.
5. In Scripture, I delight not in the blood of bullocks. Isaiah 1. The blood of bulls and of goats. Heb. 9.
corruption_summary: The sacrificial system is read either as evidence that Israel's God required appeasement like the pagan deities, or as a merely symbolic ritual with no real substitution — both of which empty the doctrine of penal substitution the bullock was given to teach.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption presents the Levitical offerings as appeasement of an angry deity, indistinguishable in kind from the sacrifices of Canaan, and then treats the New Testament's doctrine of the cross as the same primitive idea carried forward. The difference is fundamental and the texts insist on it. The pagan sacrifice is offered to a god by men seeking to change his disposition; the Levitical sacrifice is appointed by the LORD Himself, who declares in advance that He has given the blood upon the altar to make atonement. The initiative, the prescription, and the provision are all God's. That is why Isaiah can have God say He is full of the burnt offerings of rams (Isa 1:11) — He is not fed by them, was never fed by them, and never claimed to be. The offering was pedagogy in blood: a demonstration that sin costs a life.

The opposite corruption drains the offerings of any real substitution and makes them merely expressive — symbols of devotion, gifts of gratitude, with no transfer of guilt. The ritual itself forbids the reading. The offerer lays his hand on the head of the bullock, and the identification is explicit; the animal dies in his place; the blood is applied. Hebrews argues from the reality of that transaction, not against it, and its whole case is how much more: if the blood of bulls sanctified to the purifying of the flesh (Heb 9:13), how much more shall the blood of Christ purge your conscience. The principle to recover is that the bullock was a real substitute and an insufficient one, and that its insufficiency is precisely what taught Israel to look for a better sacrifice — offered once, by a Priest who did not first need to bring a bullock for Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew par is a young bull in its prime; b'n-bāqār is a bullock the son of the herd, marking its pedigree and value; 'egel is a calf. The sin offering of the priest and of the congregation alike required the bullock.
roots_lines: Hebrew par (H6499) — a young bull or bullock; the chief animal of the sin offering and of the great burnt offerings.
Hebrew par ben-bāqār — a bullock the son of the herd; the full designation in Lev 4:3, marking the animal's value and pedigree.
Hebrew 'egel (H5695) — a calf; the animal of the golden calf and of the fatted calf, distinguished from the full-grown par.
Hebrew s'mīkâh — the laying on of the offerer's hand upon the head of the victim (Lev 4:4), the act of identification and transfer.
Greek tauros (G5022) — a bull or ox; the blood of bulls and of goats (Heb 9:13), which cannot take away sins.
usage: Of the priest's sin offering: let him bring... a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering (Lev 4:3).
Of the prophetic rebuke of mere ritual: I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats (Isa 1:11).
Of thanksgiving ranked above the offering: this also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock (Psa 69:31).
scriptures: Leviticus 4:3
If the priest that is anointed do sin according to the sin of the people; then let him bring for his sin, which he hath sinned, a young bullock without blemish unto the LORD for a sin offering.
Isaiah 1:11

To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the LORD: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats.
Psalm 69:31
This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs.
Hebrews 9:13
For if the blood of bulls and of goats, and the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean, sanctifieth to the purifying of the flesh:

etymology: From Old English heord, a company of beasts. Hebrew distinguishes sharply between the bāqār, the herd of cattle, and the tsō'n, the flock of sheep and goats, and the King James keeps the distinction throughout — flocks and herds being the standard pairing for the whole of a pastoral man's living. To lose both was to lose everything.
biblical_def: The herd is the substance of a pastoral people, and Scripture uses it to measure both blessing and loss. Abram and Lot separate because the land could not carry two men's wealth: “And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents” (Gen 13:5) — the herd is what forces the choice that will take Lot to Sodom. Under the covenant the herd is one of the named tokens of God's favour: “he will also bless the fruit of thy womb, and the fruit of thy land, thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil, the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep” (Deu 7:13). Which makes the great confession of Habakkuk the more remarkable, since he deliberately strips away every one of those tokens before he states his joy: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls” (Hab 3:17) — and the verse that follows is yet I will rejoice in the LORD. The prophet names the empty stall and rejoices anyway, which is the whole doctrine of faith in one sentence. The herd is also the figure under which God describes His own care and His own judging, distinguishing between one beast and another within the same herd: “Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle” (Eze 34:22).
webster_summary: A collection of beasts feeding or driven together, particularly of the larger cattle as distinguished from a flock of sheep; in Scripture the substance of a pastoral household, a token of covenant blessing, and the empty stall of Habakkuk's faith.
webster_full: HERD, n. 1. A collection or assemblage of beasts, feeding or driven together.
2. Applied chiefly to the larger cattle, as oxen and kine; a flock being of sheep or goats.
3. A company of men, in contempt; the rabble; the vulgar herd.
4. In Scripture, flocks and herds, the whole substance of a pastoral people. Gen. 13.
5. There shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the LORD. Hab. 3.
corruption_summary: Covenant blessing is converted into a guaranteed formula of material increase, so that prosperity becomes the proof of God's favour and loss the proof of His displeasure — a doctrine Habakkuk explicitly refuses.
corruption_paragraphs: Deu 7:13 and the like promises are the raw material of every prosperity doctrine: because God promised increase of kine and flocks to a covenant nation in a particular land under particular terms, it is inferred that material abundance is the standing entitlement of faith, and that the believer who lacks it must be deficient in it. Two things are wrong with the inference. The promises were made to national Israel under the Mosaic covenant, with corresponding national curses attached in the same passage; and the New Testament transposes the blessings, telling believers plainly that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God, and that all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. The apostles were not men with full stalls, and Paul learned both how to be abased and how to abound.

Hab 3:17 is the decisive text, and it is decisive because the prophet enumerates the covenant tokens one by one and removes them: no blossom, no fruit, no oil, no meat, no flock, no herd. That is the covenant blessing catalogue read backwards, and he says yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. He does not claim the losses will be reversed, nor argue that they are unreal; he grounds joy in the LORD Himself rather than in His gifts. The principle to recover is that God's goodness is not measured by the contents of the stall, and that a faith which requires the herd to be there has never yet been tested. The opposite error — treating poverty as itself a virtue — Scripture equally denies; the herds were a genuine blessing, given and taken by the same hand.
roots_summary: Hebrew bāqār is the herd of oxen, distinguished from tsō'n, the flock of sheep and goats; 'ēder is a drove or flock generally. Greek agelē is a herd, used in the Gospels of the swine at Gadara.
roots_lines: Hebrew bāqār (H1241) — herd, oxen, cattle of the larger sort; paired constantly with tsō'n to mean a man's whole living.
Hebrew tsō'n (H6629) — the flock of sheep and goats; the smaller cattle, and the figure under which God's people are most often described.
Hebrew 'ēder (H5739) — a drove, flock, or herd; used of the flocks Jacob divided and of the tower of the flock (Mic 4:8).
Hebrew miqneh (H4735) — cattle as acquired substance; Lot also... had flocks, and herds, and tents (Gen 13:5).
Greek agelē (G34) — a herd; used only of the herd of swine into which the legion was permitted to go (Mar 5:11).
usage: Of pastoral substance forcing a choice: Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents (Gen 13:5).
Of covenant blessing: he will also bless... the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep (Deu 7:13).
Of faith with the stall empty: there shall be no herd in the stalls (Hab 3:17), followed by yet I will rejoice in the LORD.
scriptures: Genesis 13:5
And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents.
Deuteronomy 7:13

And he will love thee, and bless thee, and multiply thee: he will also bless the fruit of thy womb, and the fruit of thy land, thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil, the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep, in the land which he sware unto thy fathers to give thee.
Habakkuk 3:17

Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:
Ezekiel 34:22
Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle.

etymology: From Old English assa, ultimately from Latin asinus. The Hebrew chamōr is the male ass, probably from a root meaning reddish, the colour of the common Palestinian donkey; 'āthōn is the she-ass, the more valuable riding animal. The ass is an unclean beast under the law and yet is the mount of judges, of kings in peace, and at the last of the King Himself — a combination that carries the whole doctrine of lowliness the word is used to teach.
biblical_def: The ass is the beast of burden and of peace, and Scripture gives it a dignity the horse never receives. The horse in the Old Testament is the animal of war and of trust in armies; the ass is what a man rides when he comes in peace. That distinction governs the great messianic prophecy, where the King's arrival is announced with a deliberately humble mount: “Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass” (Zec 9:9) — fulfilled to the letter on Palm Sunday, when the Lord Jesus deliberately chose the animal that declared what kind of king He was. The ass is also unclean, and so cannot be offered; the law therefore makes a startling provision, requiring that its firstborn be bought back by the death of a clean animal or else destroyed: “And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb; and if thou wilt not redeem it, then thou shalt break his neck: and all the firstborn of man among thy children shalt thou redeem” (Exo 13:13). The unclean creature lives only because a lamb dies in its place, and the verse sets the redemption of a man's children in the same breath. Scripture also uses the ass to humble the prophet who thought he saw: “And the LORD opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times?” (Num 22:28) — the beast saw the angel the seer could not. And Proverbs puts it in a list of things governed by what they will answer to: “A whip for the horse, a bridle for the ass, and a rod for the fool's back” (Pro 26:3).
webster_summary: A well-known beast of burden, patient and sure-footed, unclean under the law; in Scripture the mount of peace as the horse is of war, the beast redeemed by a lamb, the animal that rebuked Balaam, and the mount of the King entering Zion.
webster_full: ASS, n. 1. A quadruped of the equine genus, having long slouching ears, a short mane, and a tail covered with long hairs at the end.
2. The ass is patient and sure-footed, and is used as a beast of burden, and in the east as a riding animal of dignity.
3. A dull, heavy, stupid fellow; a dolt; used in reproach.
4. Under the law an unclean beast, which might not be offered; its firstling was to be redeemed with a lamb, or its neck broken. Exod. 13.
5. In Scripture, thy King cometh unto thee... lowly, and riding upon an ass. Zech. 9.
corruption_summary: The talking ass of Numbers 22 is dismissed as folklore embedded in the text, and with it the whole class of miracle in which God overrules nature to rebuke a man who is professionally religious and spiritually blind.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The pressure on the word comes from the historical-critical treatment of Num 22 as a folk tale absorbed into the narrative — a charming survival rather than an event. The dictionary takes the account as history, and notes that the New Testament does the same: Peter refers to it as fact, saying the dumb ass speaking with man's voice forbad the madness of the prophet. The point of the episode is not the marvel but the reversal. The seer hired for his vision cannot see what his donkey sees, and is saved from the drawn sword of the angel by an animal he has beaten three times. God is perfectly able to make the beast wiser than the prophet, and He does it here to a man on his way to sell his gift for money.

The principle to recover concerns the mount of Zec 9:9. The prophecy specifies an ass rather than a horse, and the Lord Jesus arranged the detail deliberately, sending two disciples for the colt. The crowd that shouted Hosanna wanted a horse — a deliverer who would ride against Rome — and within the week the same city was crying crucify him, in part because He had come the way Zechariah said He would. He is still refused for the same reason. A king who arrives lowly, riding on a borrowed donkey, and whose throne is a cross, does not answer to the expectations men bring to religion; and the temptation to prefer a Christ on a war horse is not confined to the first century.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamōr is the male ass, and 'āthōn the she-ass; 'ayir is the young ass or colt, the word in Zec 9:9. Greek onos is an ass, and pōlon onou the colt of an ass.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamōr (H2543) — a male ass, probably from a root meaning reddish; the common beast of burden.
Hebrew 'āthōn (H860) — a she-ass, the more valuable riding beast; the animal Balaam rode (Num 22:28).
Hebrew 'ayir (H5895) — a young ass or colt; a colt the foal of an ass (Zec 9:9), never yet broken to a rider.
Hebrew pe'er / peter (H6363) — that which openeth the womb, the firstling; the firstling of an ass must be redeemed with a lamb (Exo 13:13).
Greek onos (G3688) — an ass; and hupozugion (G5268), a beast under the yoke, the word Matthew uses in quoting Zechariah.
usage: Of the King's lowly entry: thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass (Zec 9:9).
Of the unclean redeemed by a lamb: every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb (Exo 13:13).
Of the beast that saw what the prophet could not: the LORD opened the mouth of the ass (Num 22:28).

pos: n. (rendering Hebrew baz, tereph, and shalāl, Greek harpagmos in cognate senses)
etymology: From Old French preie, from Latin praeda, booty or plunder. The Hebrew has two distinct pictures. Tereph is what a beast tears — the prey of a lion, torn flesh; baz and shalāl are the spoil taken in war. Scripture uses both of the helpless caught by the strong, and its recurring promise is that God takes the prey back out of the mouth that has closed on it.
biblical_def: Prey in Scripture is what the strong take from the weak, and the Bible's doctrine about it is that God is a recoverer of prey. The psalmist praises deliverance in exactly those terms: “Blessed be the LORD, who hath not given us as a prey to their teeth” (Psa 124:6) — the figure being a beast's jaws already closed. Isaiah puts the hardest form of the question, and it is a question no human power can answer well: “Shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive delivered?” (Isa 49:24). The captive in view is lawful — justly held, rightly forfeited — which makes the case hopeless on any ground of right, and the LORD's answer in the next verse is not that the claim is invalid but that He will contend with him that contendeth and save the children Himself. This is the very shape of redemption: not a denial that sinners are justly held, but a Redeemer who takes them out of a lawful captivity by satisfying it. Ezekiel applies the same promise to a flock ruined by its own shepherds, and the remedy has two halves that are easily separated and must not be: “Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle” (Eze 34:22). God rescues the preyed-upon and He judges within the flock, distinguishing between the beast that pushed with side and shoulder and the lean sheep that was thrust away.
webster_summary: Spoil taken in war; plunder; that which is seized by violence; and the animal torn and devoured by a beast — whence in Scripture the helpless given as prey to teeth, the lawful captive God delivers, and the flock He saves from being a prey.
webster_full: PREY, n. 1. Spoil; booty; plunder; goods taken by force from an enemy in war.
2. That which is seized by violence; that which is taken as plunder or spoil.
3. Ravage; depredation; the act of seizing and devouring.
4. An animal seized and devoured by a beast of prey; as, the lion tears his prey.
5. In Scripture, given as a prey to their teeth. Psalm 124. Shall the prey be taken from the mighty? Isaiah 49.
corruption_summary: Redemption is presented either as God waiving a just claim, so that no satisfaction is made and justice is set aside, or as a transaction with the devil, as though the ransom were paid to the captor rather than to God.
corruption_paragraphs: Isa 49:24 poses the problem the atonement exists to solve, and it does so by conceding the captor's title: the captive is lawful. Sinners are not held by mistake. The common modern account of forgiveness bypasses this entirely, presenting God as simply declining to press the charge — the prey released because the claim is dropped. Scripture will not have it. God is declared to be just and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus, and the whole force of that sentence is that the claim was not waived but satisfied. A pardon that costs nothing tells the sinner that his sin was never serious, which is the opposite of the comfort the gospel offers; and it leaves the God who by no means clears the guilty in contradiction with Himself.

The opposite error, older and periodically revived, is the ransom-to-Satan theory — that the price of redemption was paid to the captor, as though the devil held rights over the elect which God was obliged to honour. Scripture describes the offering as made to God: Christ gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour, and it pleased the LORD to bruise him. Satan is a jailer with no claim, a defeated accuser whose accusations are answered at the throne, and the deliverance is described as a spoiling of principalities rather than a purchase from them. The principle to recover holds both halves of the promise in Eze 34:22: God saves His flock from being a prey, and He judges between cattle and cattle — the same act that rescues the oppressed calls the oppressor to account.
roots_summary: Hebrew tereph is torn flesh, the prey of a beast; baz and shalāl are spoil or booty taken in war; malqōach is that which is taken. The recurring promise is of prey recovered out of the mouth of the strong.
roots_lines: Hebrew tereph (H2964) — torn flesh, prey; from tāraph, to tear in pieces; the young lions roar after their prey (Psa 104:21).
Hebrew baz (H957) — spoil, plunder, booty; and shalāl (H7998), spoil taken in war, divided among the victors.
Hebrew malqōach (H4455) — that which is taken, prey or booty; shall the prey be taken from the mighty (Isa 49:24).
Hebrew gā'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; the office by which what was lost or seized is bought back.
Greek harpazō (G726) — to seize or snatch away; neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand (Joh 10:28) denies the wolf his prey.
usage: Of deliverance from the closing jaws: blessed be the LORD, who hath not given us as a prey to their teeth (Psa 124:6).
Of the lawful captive: shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive delivered? (Isa 49:24).
Of the flock saved and the flock judged: they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle (Eze 34:22).
scriptures: Psalm 124:6
Blessed be the LORD, who hath not given us as a prey to their teeth.
Isaiah 49:24
Shall the prey be taken from the mighty, or the lawful captive delivered?
Ezekiel 34:22
Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle.
Proverbs 31:8
Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.

etymology: From Old Norse vaengr. The Hebrew kānāph means a wing, and also an edge, border, or skirt of a garment — the two senses being joined by the idea of that which extends and covers. This double meaning is doctrinally important: when Ruth asks Boaz to spread his skirt over her, she uses the same word she has just heard applied to the wings of the God of Israel under which she has come to trust, and the request is a deliberate echo.
biblical_def: The wing in Scripture is the standing image of protective covering, and it belongs first to God. The psalm of protection puts it in terms of a bird sheltering its young: “He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler” (Psa 91:4). Boaz uses the figure to describe Ruth's conversion, and the Hebrew wordplay is exact, since the same noun means both a wing and the skirt of a garment: “The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust” (Rut 2:12) — and Boaz will himself become the answer to his own prayer by spreading his skirt over her as kinsman-redeemer. The exodus is described in the same terms, with the emphasis falling on the destination rather than the rescue: “Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself” (Exo 19:4). God did not merely carry Israel out; He carried them to Himself. The most affecting use is the Lord's lament over the city that would not be sheltered: “how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” (Mat 23:37) — the wing offered and refused. And Malachi promises the wing that heals, closing the Old Testament with a sunrise: unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings (Mal 4:2).
webster_summary: The limb by which a bird flies; the border, edge, or skirt of a garment; and in Scripture the wings of God under which His people take refuge, the eagles' wings that bore Israel to Himself, and the healing in the wings of the Sun of righteousness.
webster_full: WING, n. 1. The limb of a fowl or other animal, by which it flies.
2. The flight; passage by the wing; as, to take wing.
3. Means of flying or of rapid motion; as, on the wings of the wind. Psalm 18.
4. In Hebrew, the edge, border, or skirt of a garment; also the extremity of a country or of the earth.
5. In Scripture, under his wings shalt thou trust. Psalm 91. As a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings. Matt. 23.
corruption_summary: The promise of covering under God's wings is turned into a guarantee of exemption from harm in this life, so that Psalm 91 is made a charm against calamity rather than a promise of God's ultimate keeping.
corruption_paragraphs: Psa 91 is regularly read as a warrant that no evil of any kind may touch the believer — no illness, no accident, no violence — and is quoted in that sense over the sick and the endangered. The devil read it that way first. At the temptation he cited this very psalm, urging Christ to throw Himself down because it is written he shall give his angels charge over thee; and the Lord answered not by denying the promise but by refusing the use: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. That exchange is the authoritative interpretation. The psalm is not a mechanism for compelling God's protection or a licence for presumption, and the martyrs to whom it was read did not thereby escape. What it promises is that no evil shall ultimately befall the man whose dwelling is the Most High — a promise the New Testament restates as the certainty that all things work together for good.

The opposite corruption is to conclude, since believers do suffer, that the language of covering is merely poetic consolation with nothing behind it. Mat 23:37 forbids that reduction, because the offer there is real enough to be genuinely refused — how often would I have gathered thy children, and ye would not. The wing was extended and Jerusalem declined it, which is the language of an actual and rejected mercy rather than a figure of speech. The principle to recover is that the covering is real, is a Person, and is entered by trust rather than claimed as immunity: under whose wings thou art come to trust (Rut 2:12) is said of a widowed foreigner who had lost everything and found the God of Israel.
roots_summary: Hebrew kānāph means wing, and also edge, border, or skirt of a garment; the double sense links God's sheltering wings with the kinsman's spread skirt. Greek pterux is a wing, used in the Lord's lament over Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Hebrew kānāph (H3671) — wing; also the edge, border, or skirt of a garment, and the extremity of the earth.
Hebrew pāras kānāph — to spread the skirt over, the formal act of a kinsman claiming a widow (Rut 3:9), using the same noun as Rut 2:12.
Hebrew tsītsīth — the fringe commanded on the four kānāph, corners, of the garment (Num 15:38); the border the woman touched (Mat 9:20).
Greek pterux (G4420) — a wing; as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings (Mat 23:37).
Hebrew k'ruvīm — the cherubim, whose outstretched wings covered the mercy seat, the visible figure of the covering God promises.

Of the convert's trust: the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust (Rut 2:12).
Of the covering offered and refused: as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not (Mat 23:37).

etymology: From Old English corn, cognate with Latin granum, a grain. In the King James Version and in British usage generally, corn means grain of any kind — wheat, barley, spelt — and never the American maize, which was unknown in the ancient Near East and in 1611. This is one of the archaisms most likely to mislead a modern reader: the fields the disciples walked through were fields of wheat.
biblical_def: Corn is grain, the staple of life, and Scripture uses it for the ordinary providence by which God feeds the world and for the extraordinary way He saves it. In the famine it is the commodity that draws the nations to the man they had sold into slavery: “And all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands” (Gen 41:57) — the brothers' treachery becoming the means of the world's bread. The law surrounding corn is notable for its gentleness toward the labourer, including the animal one: “Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn” (Deu 25:4), a verse Paul twice applies to the maintenance of gospel ministers, arguing that God's care in such a matter was written for our sakes. The growth of corn is the Lord's figure for the hidden, unforced progress of the kingdom: “For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear” (Mar 4:28) — a sequence no farmer can hurry and none can fully explain. And the cornfield is the setting of one of the great sabbath controversies, where hunger, mercy, and the Lord's authority over the day are all at issue at once: “At that time Jesus went on the sabbath day through the corn; and his disciples were an hungred, and began to pluck the ears of corn, and to eat” (Mat 12:1). The single grain finally becomes the figure of His own death, for except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone.
webster_summary: Grain of any kind — wheat, barley, rye — and never maize in the Authorized Version; in Scripture the staple of life, the sheaf of the firstfruits, the field of the sabbath controversy, and the single grain that must die to bear fruit.
webster_full: CORN, n. 1. A single seed of certain plants, as wheat, rye, barley and maize; a grain.
2. In Great Britain, corn is a general term for all sorts of grain used for bread; wheat, rye, barley and oats.
3. The plants which produce corn, when growing in the field; as a field of corn.
4. In Scripture usage, grain in general; the harvest of the field, the staple of bread. Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn. Deut. 25.
5. Corn and wine and oil; the standing summary of the produce of the land, and a token of covenant blessing. Deut. 7.
corruption_summary: The ordinary providence by which God feeds the world through seedtime and harvest is treated as an impersonal mechanism, so that daily bread ceases to be received as a gift and thanksgiving becomes a formality.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is practical secularism about food. Because the process from seed to loaf is understood, it is felt to be self-explaining, and the hand of God is looked for only in what science has not yet accounted for — a habit which shrinks God into the gaps and guarantees His steady eviction. Scripture never distinguishes the ordinary from the divine in this way. The Lord Jesus, teaching men to ask for daily bread, was speaking to farmers who knew exactly how wheat grows, and He grounds the doctrine of providence in the most regular phenomena there are: God maketh his sun to rise, sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust, and clothes the grass of the field. Mar 4:28 explicitly presents the growth of corn as something that happens while the farmer sleeps and which he knoweth not how — the mechanism understood and the giving still God's.

The principle to recover is that thanksgiving is the appropriate response to a mechanism, not a substitute for understanding one. Paul makes the refusal of thanks a mark of the fallen mind — when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful — and commends every creature of God as good if it be received with thanksgiving. There is a second recovery in Deu 25:4: God legislates for the comfort of an ox on a threshing floor, and Paul argues from that verse to the support of ministers, which tells us both that no detail of God's law is beneath notice and that the God who will not have an ox muzzled at his work does not intend His servants to labour unfed.
roots_summary: Hebrew dāgān is corn or grain generally, standing with wine and oil for the produce of the land; bār is threshed grain. Greek sitos is wheat or grain, and kokkos is a single seed or kernel.
roots_lines: Hebrew dāgān (H1715) — corn, grain; paired with tīrōsh (new wine) and yits'hār (oil) as the produce of the land.
Hebrew bār (H1250) — threshed and winnowed grain; the corn Joseph stored and sold (Gen 41:57).
Hebrew 'ābīb (H24) — green ears of corn; whence the month Abib, the month of ripening ears, in which the Passover falls.
Greek sitos (G4621) — wheat or grain; gather the wheat into my barn (Mat 13:30).
Greek kokkos (G2848) — a grain or kernel; except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die (Joh 12:24).
usage: Of providence in famine: all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn (Gen 41:57).
Of mercy to the labouring beast: thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn (Deu 25:4).
Of the kingdom's hidden growth: first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear (Mar 4:28).

etymology: From Old English gaers, of the same root as grow and green. The Hebrew chātsīr is the green herbage of the field, and in the Palestinian climate its life is startlingly brief: the spring growth that carpets the hills after the rains is scorched brown within weeks by the east wind. The biblical figure is therefore not a general observation about mortality but a description of something the writers watched happen every year.
biblical_def: Grass is Scripture's standing figure for the brevity of man, and it is used with a severity that is meant to be heard. Isaiah is commissioned to preach it as his message, and the commission is given in the form of a question and answer: “The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6). It is not only human weakness that is compared to grass but human goodliness — the beauty, achievement, and strength that men suppose will last. The psalmist says the same with more tenderness, and immediately grounds comfort in the contrast: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15), the next verses turning to the mercy of the LORD which is from everlasting to everlasting. Peter quotes Isaiah for the express purpose of setting the perishable against the imperishable: “For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away” (1Pe 1:24) — and the verse following is but the word of the Lord endureth for ever. The doctrine is not despair but proportion. And the Lord Jesus takes the same short-lived grass and makes it an argument for confidence rather than dread: “Wherefore, if God so clothe the grass of the field, which to day is, and to morrow is cast into the oven, shall he not much more clothe you, O ye of little faith?” (Mat 6:30). God spends real beauty on what lasts a fortnight and is then used for fuel; He will not neglect His children.
webster_summary: Herbage; the green covering of the fields, proverbially short-lived under the eastern sun; in Scripture the figure of the brevity of all flesh and of human glory, set against the abiding word of the Lord, and the argument for God's care of His people.
webster_full: GRASS, n. 1. In common usage, herbage; the plants which constitute the food of cattle and other beasts.
2. In botany, a plant having simple leaves, a stem generally jointed and tubular, and the husk or calyx composed of glumes.
3. The green herbage of the field, which springs quickly and as quickly withers under the eastern sun.
4. In Scripture, a figure of the frailty and short continuance of man and of his glory. All flesh is grass. Isaiah 40.
5. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever. Isaiah 40; 1 Pet. 1.
corruption_summary: Human mortality is either denied outright by a culture that hides death and promises indefinite extension, or made an occasion for despair — both of which miss the use Scripture makes of the figure, which is to fix hope on what does not wither.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live corruption is the studied refusal to reckon with mortality: death removed from the home to the institution, age treated as a medical failure rather than a season, and the tacit promise that sufficient technique will indefinitely postpone the withering. Scripture's counsel runs directly against it — so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom — and treats the refusal to number them as folly rather than optimism. The rich fool had many goods laid up for many years and had not counted the one night. To say all flesh is grass is not morbidity; it is accuracy, and accuracy is the beginning of wisdom about how a life should be spent.

The opposite reaction takes the figure and stops there, concluding that if man is grass then nothing he does matters. Neither Isaiah nor Peter stops there. In both places the sentence about grass exists to set up its antithesis: but the word of our God shall stand for ever, and Peter adds, and this is the word which by the gospel is preached unto you. The point is not that everything perishes but that one thing does not, and that a man may attach himself to it. The Lord Jesus completes the argument in the gentlest direction of all (Mat 6:30): the God who lavishes beauty on grass destined for the oven is not going to neglect His children, so that the brevity of the flower becomes a reason to stop being anxious rather than a reason to despair.
roots_summary: Hebrew chātsīr is green herbage or grass, proverbially short-lived; deshe' is tender new growth; 'ēseb is herb or vegetation. Greek chortos is grass, herbage, or fodder.
roots_lines: Hebrew chātsīr (H2682) — grass, green herbage; the figure of frailty in Isa 40:6 and Psa 103:15.
Hebrew deshe' (H1877) — tender grass, the first green growth; let the earth bring forth grass (Gen 1:11).
Hebrew 'ēseb (H6212) — herb, vegetation; the herb of the field which man was sentenced to eat (Gen 3:18).
Greek chortos (G5528) — grass, herbage, fodder; the grass of the field which to day is (Mat 6:30).
Greek anthos (G438) — a flower or blossom; the flower of grass that falleth away (1Pe 1:24), quoting Isaiah.
usage: Of the prophet's commissioned message: all flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field (Isa 40:6).
Of the contrast with the abiding word: the grass withereth... but the word of the Lord endureth for ever (1Pe 1:24-25).
Of the argument from the lesser to the greater: if God so clothe the grass of the field... shall he not much more clothe you (Mat 6:30).

etymology: From Old English faett. The Hebrew chēleb denotes the hard suet about the kidneys and inwards of a sacrificial animal, and it was regarded as the richest part — which is why the law reserves it wholly to God and forbids Israel to eat it. From the sacrificial sense the word extends to mean the best of anything: the fat of the land is its choicest produce, and to be fat is to be prosperous.
biblical_def: Fat in Scripture is the choicest portion, and the law puts it beyond human use with a formula of striking simplicity: “And the priest shall burn them upon the altar: it is the food of the offering made by fire for a sweet savour: all the fat is the LORD'S” (Lev 3:16). The best is reserved to God, not as something He needs but as a daily lesson in what worship costs. From that the word becomes a figure for abundance, and also for the peculiar spiritual danger abundance brings. The song of Moses uses it to describe a nation ruined by its own prosperity, in a line whose bluntness has never been improved on: “But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation” (Deu 32:15). Prosperity did what persecution could not. The prophets then use the word against the very offerings it belonged to, when the offerings are brought by unrepentant men: “I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks” (Isa 1:11). And Samuel states the ranking that governs the whole sacrificial system, in the sentence that broke Saul: “Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). The fat was God's by law; obedience was God's by right, and the man who offered the one while withholding the other had given Him nothing.
webster_summary: The oily concrete substance of animal bodies; in the Levitical law the suet of the sacrifice, reserved wholly to the LORD and forbidden as food; and by extension the best or choicest part — whence the fat of the land, and the fatness that made Jeshurun kick.
webster_full: FAT, n. 1. A solid oily concrete substance, found in the cellular membrane of animal bodies.
2. The best or richest part of a thing; as the fat of the land. Gen. 45.
3. adj. Fleshy; plump; corpulent; abounding with fat.
4. Rich; wealthy; affluent; as, a fat benefice. Also, fertile; as fat land.
5. In the Levitical law, the suet of the inwards, wholly consumed on the altar; all the fat is the LORD's. Levit. 3. Ye shall eat no manner of fat. Levit. 7.
corruption_summary: Prosperity is treated as an unambiguous sign of God's approval rather than as one of the most dangerous conditions a soul can be in, so that the warning of Jeshurun waxing fat is never applied to the comfortable.
corruption_paragraphs: Deu 32:15 describes a sequence that Scripture treats as ordinary rather than exceptional: God prospers a people, the people grow thick with prosperity, and then they forsake the God who prospered them. Jeshurun — the affectionate name for upright Israel — kicked. Agur asks to be given neither poverty nor riches for exactly this reason: lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? Where prosperity is read simply as approval, this entire strand of biblical warning becomes unusable, and the comfortable are deprived of the one diagnosis most likely to fit them. The Laodicean church said I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing, and did not know it was wretched and poor and blind and naked; the danger of fatness is precisely that it is invisible from inside.

The second corruption concerns worship, and 1Sa 15:22 is its cure. Saul had kept back the best of the spoil, intending to sacrifice it, and the reply he received sets the whole sacrificial system in its place: to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Religious generosity offered in place of obedience is not a partial payment but a substitution God refuses, and it remains one of the commonest evasions in devout circles — giving abundantly, serving visibly, and withholding the one thing commanded. The principle to recover is the law's own: all the fat is the LORD'S (Lev 3:16). The best belongs to Him by right, and a man who brings Him the fat while keeping back his obedience has inverted the order and given God the cheaper thing.
roots_summary: Hebrew chēleb is the suet or fat of a sacrifice, reserved to the LORD and forbidden as food; shāmēn means fat, rich, or fertile; mishmān is fatness or richness of soil.
roots_lines: Hebrew chēleb (H2459) — the fat or suet about the kidneys and inwards; all the fat is the LORD'S (Lev 3:16), and Israel was forbidden to eat it.
Hebrew shāmēn (H8082) — fat, rich, fertile; used of good land, of well-fed beasts, and of prosperous men.
Hebrew Y'shurūn (H3484) — the upright one, a poetic name for Israel; Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked (Deu 32:15).
Hebrew chēleb hā'ārets — the fat of the land, its choicest produce; promised to Jacob's household in Egypt (Gen 45:18).
Hebrew shāma' (H8085) — to hear and so to obey; to hearken is better than the fat of rams (1Sa 15:22).
usage: Of the portion reserved to God: all the fat is the LORD'S (Lev 3:16).
Of prosperity as a spiritual danger: Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked... then he forsook God which made him (Deu 32:15).
Of obedience ranked above offering: to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams (1Sa 15:22).

etymology: From Old Norse skinn, a hide. The Hebrew 'ōr means skin or hide, of man or beast, and is the word for the coats God made for Adam and Eve. It is worth noting that it is not the same word as 'ōr meaning light, though the two are spelled alike in English transliteration — a coincidence that has produced a good deal of fanciful preaching about Adam losing a garment of light, for which the Hebrew gives no warrant.
biblical_def: Skin in Scripture is the boundary of a man — the last thing between him and the world — and its first appearance in the Bible is a mercy purchased by death. Adam and Eve had sewn fig leaves; God replaced them: “Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them” (Gen 3:21). Something died in Eden to clothe them, and the covering God provides replaces the covering man contrives — the first sacrifice and the first gospel picture, told in a single verse without comment. Skin is also the measure of extremity in affliction. Job, stripped of everything, describes what is left of him: “My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth” (Job 19:20) — and it is out of that condition, not out of comfort, that he says I know that my redeemer liveth. Satan had earlier used skin as his cynical formula for what a man will trade to survive: “Skin for skin, yea, all that a man hath will he give for his life” (Job 2:4), a proposition the whole book is written to disprove. Jeremiah then uses skin for the one thing about a man that cannot be altered by effort, and makes it a picture of the will in bondage to sin: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23) — the answer being no, which is why regeneration must be a work of God. And when a man has been with God the change shows on the skin without his knowing it: Moses wist not that the skin of his face shone (Exo 34:29).
webster_summary: The natural covering of animal bodies; a hide; and in Scripture the coats of skins God made for Adam, the skin of the teeth by which Job escaped, the skin the Ethiopian cannot change, and the shining skin of Moses' face.
webster_full: SKIN, n. 1. The natural covering of animal bodies, consisting of the cuticle or scarf-skin, and the cutis or true skin.
2. A hide; the pelt of a beast, used for leather or clothing. Coats of skins. Gen. 3.
3. The exterior coat of fruits and plants; the rind.
4. A vessel made of skin, used for holding liquors; a bottle. New wine into old bottles. Matt. 9.
5. In Scripture, I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. Job 19. Can the Ethiopian change his skin? Jer. 13.
corruption_summary: Skin colour is made the fundamental category of human identity and moral standing, in place of the biblical categories of one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ; and Jeremiah's image of unchangeable skin is wrenched from its subject, which is the bondage of the will.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture's anthropology has no category corresponding to modern race. It knows one blood — God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth — and it locates the deep human division not between peoples but between Adam and Christ. Frameworks which make inherited skin colour the determinant of guilt, innocence, or standing therefore replace the Bible's categories rather than applying them, and they do so in both directions: the older error that used ancestry to justify contempt and bondage, and the current one that assigns moral standing by group membership. Both are answered by the same texts. There is no difference: for all have sinned; and in Christ there is neither Greek nor Jew, Barbarian, Scythian, bond nor free.

Jer 13:23 is separately abused, being quoted as a proverb about the futility of change in general or, worse, as though the Ethiopian's skin were the thing needing alteration. The prophet's subject is stated in the second half of his own sentence: then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil. The comparison is to habit hardened into nature, and its doctrine is the bondage of the will — that a man accustomed to evil can no more reform himself than a leopard can rearrange its spots. That is not a counsel of despair but the reason the new birth must be a work of God: except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. The principle to recover is the one Gen 3:21 sets at the very beginning: the covering a man makes for himself is inadequate, and the covering that works is one God provides at the cost of a life.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'ōr is skin or hide, of man or beast; it is the material of the coats God made in Eden and of the tabernacle's outer coverings. Greek derma is skin, and dermatinos means made of skin, as of John the Baptist's girdle.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ōr (H5785) — skin, hide, leather; coats of skins (Gen 3:21) and the badgers' skins covering the tabernacle.
Hebrew bāsār (H1320) — flesh; paired with skin in Job's description of his wasted body (Job 19:20).
Hebrew qāran (H7160) — to send out rays, to shine; the skin of his face shone (Exo 34:29), the verb also meaning to send out horns.
Greek derma (G1192) — skin, hide; and dermatinos (G1193), made of skin, of the leathern girdle of John the Baptist.
Greek askos (G779) — a leathern bottle or wineskin; the old bottles which new wine would burst (Mat 9:17).
usage: Of the first covering God provided: unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them (Gen 3:21).
Of the extremity of affliction: I am escaped with the skin of my teeth (Job 19:20).
Of the will's bondage: can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? (Jer 13:23).
scriptures: Genesis 3:21
Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.
My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.
Job 2:4
